Start by separating encoding from ID generation. A Base62 encoder only converts an ID into a compact URL-safe string; uniqueness comes from the underlying ID. For a distributed system, a Snowflake-style 64-bit generator is a strong choice: timestamp + worker identity + sequence produce unique IDs independently on many servers. Base62-encode the generated ID. Alternatives are random Base62 strings with collision checks, or a central counter for a simpler system. Avoid assuming that truncating a hash makes collisions impossible.

Enforce a unique constraint on shortCode in the database. Generate a candidate, attempt an atomic insert, and if the unique constraint fails, generate another candidate and retry with a bounded retry policy. The database uniqueness constraint is the final correctness guard. As the namespace fills, collision probability rises, so choose sufficient code length rather than relying on endless retries.

Use shortCode as the cache key because it is exactly what the redirect request provides. Store longUrl as the minimum value; optionally store status, expiresAt, or a version. The redirect service first checks Redis and falls back to the database on a miss, then populates the cache.

Use a bounded Redis memory policy appropriate to the workload, commonly LRU/LFU-like behavior, plus TTLs for freshness and memory reclamation. TTLs should be jittered so large groups of entries do not expire simultaneously. If links themselves expire, the cache TTL must never outlive the authoritative expiresAt.

A single hot key is not solved merely by sharding because all requests for that key still map to one shard/cache owner. Add layers that replicate the value: local in-memory caches on app servers, Redis read replicas where appropriate, and edge/CDN caching for redirects. Protect refill with request coalescing. At extreme scale, replicate the hot object deliberately rather than trying to partition one key.

When many requests miss the same key concurrently, designate one in-flight request as the leader. Only that request fetches the database value; the others wait for its result. The leader fills Redis and shares the result. This prevents thousands of identical DB reads after one hot key expires. Within one process this is often called single-flight; across processes you need distributed coordination or another shared caching layer.

Instead of giving every cache entry exactly the same TTL, add a small random component, for example baseTTL ± a bounded random amount. That spreads expiration times and reduces a cache avalanche in which many keys become misses simultaneously.

Receive GET /{shortCode}; validate the code; check local cache if present, then Redis. On hit, validate status/expiry and redirect. On Redis miss, route to the correct DB shard using shortCode, fetch the mapping, validate it, populate Redis, emit analytics asynchronously, and return 301 or 302. If absent, return 404; if a previously valid resource is intentionally gone/expired, 410 can be considered depending on API semantics.

Redirect requests contain shortCode, so indexing directly on it makes the dominant lookup efficient. If the table instead uses an internal ID as the primary key, shortCode still needs a unique secondary index. At large scale, using shortCode as the logical shard key also lets the service route directly to the correct shard.

Use 301 when the destination is truly permanent and you are comfortable with browsers/proxies caching the redirect, reducing future traffic to your service. Use 302 when you want clients to continue contacting the shortener, which preserves control over destination changes and server-side click measurement. Many shorteners favor temporary redirects for control, even when the target rarely changes.

Hash the shortCode and route based on the hash. Hash sharding avoids the sequential-write hotspot that range-sharding monotonically increasing IDs can create. The mapping should be deterministic so any application server can calculate the destination shard.

Simple hash(key) mod N causes widespread remapping when N changes. Consistent hashing maps both keys and shards onto a ring so membership changes move only neighboring key ranges. Virtual nodes place each physical shard at many points on the ring, improving balance and making rebalancing smoother.

Replicate every shard. If the leader fails, promote a healthy replica and update routing/metadata. Reads may continue from replicas if the consistency model permits. The system also needs health checks, automated failover, backups, and a recovery procedure for a full shard loss.

Do not immediately return 404 from a lagging replica. After the primary write succeeds, populate Redis so immediate redirects usually hit cache. For stronger read-after-write behavior, route the creator’s subsequent reads to the leader for a short period, or on replica miss fall back to the primary before declaring the code absent.

NTP reduces drift but the generator must detect rollback. Compare current time to the last timestamp used. If current time is behind, wait until the clock catches up, temporarily reject generation, or use a safe logical/fallback mechanism. Worker IDs must also be unique; two generators using the same worker ID can create duplicates even with correct clocks.

Yes. Base62 is reversible encoding, and sequential/time-structured IDs can be enumerable. This is acceptable if short URLs are public identifiers and enumeration is not a security boundary. If unpredictability matters, use cryptographically random codes or an obfuscating permutation/encryption layer before encoding, while still enforcing uniqueness.

Creation can be abused for spam, phishing, malware, or resource exhaustion; redirects can be brute-forced. Apply rate limits, authentication/API quotas where relevant, URL reputation or malware scanning, domain/block lists, CAPTCHA for anonymous high-risk creation, and monitoring. Treat the short code as an identifier, not an authorization secret unless it is generated with sufficient entropy and the product explicitly relies on secrecy.

Mark/delete the mapping in the authoritative DB and invalidate all relevant cache layers. A tombstone is often safer than immediate physical deletion because it can propagate “this code is gone” and prevent stale replicas/caches from resurrecting it. Multi-region systems may publish an invalidation event and include version/status metadata in cached values.

Use global traffic management to route users to nearby healthy regions. Serve redirects from regional caches/replicas for low latency. Choose a write topology: a home/primary region is simpler; multi-leader is more complex. Replicate mappings asynchronously, then handle local replica misses with a fallback to the authoritative region so replication lag does not cause false 404s.

Yes. Cache confirmed “not found” results for a short TTL so repeated invalid codes do not repeatedly cross regions or hit the DB. This is negative caching. Keep the TTL short and invalidate/update it when a code is created; otherwise a newly created mapping can be hidden behind a stale negative entry.

First avoid a single point of failure with Redis replicas/sentinel/cluster or managed failover. During a full cache outage, use local per-instance caches for hottest data, protect the DB with concurrency limits/rate limiting/load shedding, and spread reads across DB replicas where safe. When Redis returns, warm gradually instead of flooding the DB to rebuild the cache.

Accept an Idempotency-Key. Atomically claim/store it with the operation and final result. A retry with the same key returns the original short code rather than creating another. Do not automatically deduplicate solely by longUrl unless product requirements say identical long URLs must share a short code.

Use an atomic uniqueness boundary. A DB row with a unique idempotency-key constraint is robust; Redis SET NX with TTL can also elect one request as the owner. The winner creates and stores the result; losers wait/poll/read the stored result. Ensure the lock does not expire while work is still active, or use a lease-extension/fencing strategy for more rigorous designs.

Keep analytics off the synchronous redirect path. After resolving the URL, publish a small click event to Kafka or another durable queue and return the redirect without waiting for downstream aggregation. Consumers can enrich, aggregate, and persist analytics independently. This decouples redirect availability/latency from analytics storage.

Redirect availability should usually win. The producer can retry briefly and/or buffer locally if losing events is unacceptable; otherwise drop some analytics after a bounded attempt. If consumers are down but Kafka is healthy, retained events can be processed later. Design consumers to tolerate duplicates because retries and at-least-once delivery can replay events.

Store expiresAt and index it. Enforce expiry on every redirect read, so correctness never depends on cleanup. A background worker scans the expiry index in bounded batches and tombstones/deletes expired rows. Redis TTL can mirror expiry. Avoid full-table daily scans because they become increasingly expensive.

Nothing incorrect should happen. The row may remain physically present, but the redirect handler compares expiresAt with current time and returns an expired/not-found response. Cleanup is storage maintenance, not the mechanism that defines whether the link is valid.

Put a unique constraint on alias/shortCode and attempt an atomic insert. Exactly one transaction succeeds; the other receives a uniqueness conflict and returns “alias already taken.” A Redis lock is optional optimization/coordination, but the database uniqueness constraint should remain the correctness guarantee.

Keep rate-limit state in a shared low-latency store such as Redis. Use an atomic token-bucket or sliding-window algorithm keyed by user/API key/IP/tenant. Every create consumes capacity; requests beyond the policy receive HTTP 429. Token bucket permits controlled bursts while maintaining a long-term rate.

Estimate writes per second from monthly creates, reads per second from the read/write ratio, storage from mappings × bytes per row × retention, cache size from the hot working set, and network bandwidth from average request/response size. For example, 100 million creates/month is roughly 39 writes/s on average (100,000,000 / 2,592,000 seconds). If redirects are 100× writes, average redirect QPS is roughly 3,900; then apply a peak factor rather than designing only for averages.

1. Why is pasteId a good partition key?
Because the dominant access pattern is exact lookup by pasteId, and high-cardinality generated IDs distribute traffic evenly.
2. Why is object-first then metadata a safer cross-store write order?
An orphan body can be garbage-collected, but visible metadata pointing to a missing body creates a broken paste.
It guarantees short unique IDs outside the hot create path and lets app servers consume leased keys locally.
4. Why should cache TTL never exceed paste expiry?
Otherwise an expired paste could still be served from cache after its logical lifetime ended.

All reads still target one logical key; CDN/cache replication is the correct hot-key solution.

I would hash keys into many virtual-node ranges and replicate each range to N physical nodes across independent failure domains. Any stateless coordinator maps the key to its preference list, sends operations in parallel, and returns after the requested R or W responses. Replicas durably append to WAL and an LSM-style store. Version metadata distinguishes stale from concurrent values, so quorum reads can reconcile and perform read repair. During temporary failures, sloppy quorum can write to fallback nodes with hints; hinted handoff later restores intended replicas, while Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs cold divergence. Gossip/failure detection manages membership, and versioned, throttled vnode streaming handles rebalancing. If the requirement is linearizability, I would use a consensus-backed partition rather than claiming ordinary Dynamo quorum provides it.

textRun.content: Stores file details, names, and current versions.
File chunks cannot be changed once stored.
Upload only new or missing chunks.
A new version becomes visible only after the metadata is committed.
Clients use an ordered change log to stay updated.
Detect changes using the original version and preserve both edits.

Assume desktop sync is the primary deep dive. Support file/folder create, update, rename/move, delete, version history, and sharing. Files may be large, devices may go offline, and sync should be near-real-time when online.

Collaborative Google-Docs-style character-by-character editing is a different CRDT/OT problem. A Dropbox-like filesystem usually treats arbitrary files as opaque bytes and resolves concurrent offline edits at file/revision granularity.
Extremely high; user files must not disappear
Do not resend whole large files
Local DB + queued changes + conflict detection
Dedup, lifecycle, cold tiers, compression where useful

The storage-growth number is intentionally large enough to force object/blob storage. The exact number is less important than recognizing that metadata is tiny compared with file content and must scale independently.
Many candidates draw only server boxes. For Dropbox, explain what the desktop client stores and how it recovers after restart/offline periods. That is central to a realistic sync design.
Treat metadata as the control plane and file bytes as the data plane. Control-plane requests need correctness and low size; data-plane transfers need throughput, resumability, and cheap storage.
fileId, parentFolderId, name, currentRevision, owner/ACL, status
revisionId, fileId, baseRevision, chunk list, size, timestamp

If path were the identity, renaming a parent folder would conceptually rename millions of child paths. Stable IDs let the namespace update only the moved node while paths are resolved from parent relationships or indexed views.
Metadata operations such as 'rename file if target name does not already exist' are correctness-sensitive. Use a transaction/conditional write rather than eventually consistent check-then-write.
More bytes resent for small edits
Choose a few MiB as a simple baseline, then adapt by file size/workload. Tiny files may be stored as one chunk; huge files can use larger chunks to keep manifests manageable.

For a straightforward Dropbox design, fixed-size chunks are enough. Mention CDC/rsync-style rolling hashes as an optimization for workloads where small insertions into very large files would otherwise resend too much data.

Cryptographic collisions are astronomically unlikely, but correctness-sensitive systems can still verify chunk length/hash and treat a conflicting same-hash/different-content observation as a severe integrity event.
I would start with within-account or server-side dedup. I would not casually expose global chunk existence to clients because storage optimization can create a confidentiality side channel.
The metadata commit is the moment a new version exists. Chunk uploads are preparation; they do not change what other devices see until CommitUpload succeeds.
Application servers stay small and horizontally scalable because they coordinate transfers instead of proxying every byte. This reduces network cost, memory pressure, and blast radius.
The manifest is permission-sensitive metadata. The chunk data is immutable, but access to it still needs scoped authorization or signed URLs.
They simplify rollback, conflict detection, auditing, caching, and dedup. The mutable part is only the small pointer to which revision is current.
The change log is the authoritative mechanism for catching up. Real-time notifications only tell a client that it should query the change log.
Push answers WHEN to sync. The change log answers WHAT to sync.
After a 30-minute notification outage, millions of clients may reconnect at once. Design the notification layer and metadata read path for thundering-herd recovery, not only normal steady state.
Not suitable for arbitrary binary files
For arbitrary files, preserve both revisions and create a conflicted copy such as 'report (Alice's conflicted copy).docx'. Never silently overwrite one offline edit with another.

Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android have different path, case, reserved-name, and filesystem semantics. A production sync client needs a canonical server namespace plus platform-specific local translation.
Do not immediately delete a blob
A file deletion is a metadata event. Blob deletion is a later storage-management event because other revisions/users may still reference the same chunk.
Knowing a chunk hash or fileId should never be sufficient for access. Every manifest/download authorization derives from the current resource ACL/share-link state.
Use strong conditional metadata writes for namespace/revision correctness. Use immutable content and asynchronous replication for bulk bytes once the commit's durability threshold is satisfied.
Keep operations that must be atomic in the same metadata partition whenever possible. That is often more important than perfectly uniform load.
A practical service may keep newly uploaded/hot chunks replicated for fast access and later encode colder data more efficiently.
Checking only at the disk layer misses corruption elsewhere in the path. An end-to-end content hash lets the client and server agree on exactly which bytes a chunk represents.
Global plaintext-content dedup and true end-to-end encryption pull in opposite directions. State that trade-off instead of claiming you can maximize both simultaneously.
Product billing/accounting should be stable and understandable. Dedup implementation details should not leak into whether a user's 1 GB file 'counts' against quota.

Use single-writer/home-region metadata per account with multi-region blob replication. It provides a clean correctness model and is usually sufficient unless write latency in every geography is a hard requirement.
Failover; pause writes rather than risk split brain
Resume missing chunks using upload session
Chunk upload completed but no commit
Clients continue delta polling / long-poll fallback
Fail over metadata owner; serve replicated blobs
Disable new dedup optimization if safe; correctness first
When uncertain, preserve file correctness and durability even if sync becomes slower. Users tolerate delayed sync much better than corrupted or silently lost files.
A sync system lives on unreliable networks. Every operation that can be retried after timeout must either be idempotent or carry enough state to detect duplicate execution.

Optimize for the workload. Dropbox-style systems need both tiny text/config files and huge media files, so a hybrid small-file policy can reduce request overhead without forcing all content into the metadata database.
A good sync client is a bandwidth scheduler. It should be efficient without making the user's video call or active download unusable.
Serve /file/{fileId}/revision/{revId} or signed chunk URLs rather than caching an ambiguous 'latest' response forever. Immutable identifiers make CDN behavior safe.
For sync, measure convergence: how long from one device's committed revision until another healthy online device observes and applies it. Component latency alone does not measure the user experience.
Delta chunks / CDC for suitable workloads
Keep blobs out; partition by account/namespace
Do not delete old versions merely to save bytes if restore/history is a paid or trust-critical feature. Cost optimization must respect product guarantees.
Single API + SQL metadata + object storage
Explain the migration path. A correct simple service should be able to evolve into the final architecture without rewriting the product semantics.
Chunking, resumable upload, content hashes, commit

Memorize the core chain: client watcher -> chunk/hash -> upload missing chunks -> commit immutable revision -> append change log -> push hint -> other devices pull deltas -> download missing chunks. Then remember the two correctness rules: metadata commit is the visibility point, and concurrent base revisions create conflicts instead of silent overwrite.
Watcher + local DB + chunker + transfer + sync worker
Upload missing chunks -> conditional metadata commit
Push/long poll is only a hint
Compare expected base rev; preserve conflicted copy
Tombstone first; GC unreferenced chunks later
Metadata ACL + revocable high-entropy share link
TLS, encryption at rest, scoped tokens, ACL

Dropbox is a metadata-coordination system around immutable chunk storage. The client watches local files, chunks and hashes changes, uploads only missing blocks, and atomically commits a new revision using the expected base revision. The server appends every metadata mutation to an ordered per-account change log; push notifications only wake clients, which pull deltas from their durable cursors. Other devices download only missing chunks. Immutable revisions enable restore and dedup, concurrent edits become conflicted copies, deletes become tombstones before delayed GC, and permissions live in metadata while blob bytes are served through scalable object storage/CDN.
1. Why is metadata commit the visibility point?
Because all required chunks are durable first; clients never observe a revision pointing to missing content.
2. Why is path a bad permanent file identity?
Rename/move changes path, especially for whole directory subtrees; stable fileId survives these operations.
3. What does the change cursor solve?
It lets a client fetch only changes since its last known state instead of rescanning the full namespace.
4. Why are push notifications only hints?
They can be lost/duplicated/reordered; the durable change log guarantees catch-up.
5. How do you detect offline edit conflict?
Commit includes expected base revision; if current revision advanced, the edit is concurrent.
6. Why not immediately delete a chunk after one file is deleted?
Other revisions/files/users may reference that deduplicated chunk.
Each chunk is independently acknowledged/retried, so failed transfer restarts only missing blocks.
8. What is the main privacy risk of global dedup?
A dedup/existence response can reveal that known content already exists in another user's storage.
9. What should happen if push service is down?
Clients continue syncing from the change log using polling/long-poll fallback.
10. What are the two strongest correctness ideas to remember?
Strong/conditional metadata commit and conflict detection using revision ancestry instead of silent last-write-wins.

This document is intentionally self-contained. It covers the simple crawler, the scaled distributed design, URL frontier scheduling, politeness, robots.txt, deduplication, recrawling, traps, failure handling, multi-region concerns, and detailed interviewer follow-ups. The aim is to make this the only reference you need for a Web Crawler interview.
How do we continuously discover and fetch billions of web pages at high throughput while remaining polite to each host, avoiding duplicate work, surviving failures, and keeping important pages fresh?

I will design a continuous public-web crawler for HTML pages. It will respect robots.txt and per-host politeness, tolerate occasional duplicate fetches, store raw content and metadata, and prioritize important/fresh pages. Indexing and ranking are downstream systems.
Accept seed URLs and discover links recursively
~2 TB minimum, much more with indexes/history
The URL discovery rate can be tens of times larger than the page-fetch rate. Therefore deduplication and frontier admission must be extremely cheap, horizontally scalable, and mostly asynchronous.
url_id, normalized_url, host_key, priority, eligible_at, attempt

Aggressive normalization improves deduplication but risks merging distinct resources. Conservative normalization wastes crawl budget but preserves correctness. Start conservative and add domain-aware rules.
The URL frontier is a scheduler, not merely a queue. It must combine priority with politeness.

Normalize + dedupe → frontier schedules by priority and host eligibility → worker checks robots/DNS and fetches → parser stores content and emits outlinks → outlinks return through normalization/dedupe → recrawl scheduler re-injects due URLs.
Multiple priority queues or weighted queues
If 1,000 workers each keep a local '1 request/sec' counter for example.com, the aggregate can become 1,000 requests/sec. Politeness state must have a shared or uniquely owned authority.

Hash the normalized URL. Use a local/partitioned probabilistic filter to reject most repeats cheaply, then durable exact state when false positives are unacceptable. A Bloom false positive means a page may never be crawled, so tune it to the product’s acceptable miss rate.
Exactly-once network fetching is not realistic: a worker can fetch successfully and crash before recording completion. Design for occasional duplicate fetches and make downstream writes idempotent.
Do not partition only by URL hash for scheduling
Two different URL hashes from the same host could land on different workers and independently violate the host’s crawl rate. Scheduling partitioning must preserve a host-level authority.
In practice, use priority classes plus bounded scoring. It is easier to reason about starvation, freshness SLAs, and operational overrides than an unconstrained single floating-point score.
Deduplication does not solve an infinite URL generator because every generated URL may be unique. You need budgets and pattern-based trap detection.
Fail over replicated state; temporarily pause owned hosts
Buffer/retry admissions or use bounded local filters; avoid uncontrolled duplicate storm
Backpressure fetchers; do not acknowledge before durable handoff
Use valid cache entries; backoff new resolutions
Use last valid policy or conservative pause according to policy
When ownership changes, attach a monotonically increasing epoch to leases. Workers from an old epoch cannot commit scheduler state after a new owner has taken over.
Trap detection + budgets + JS render pool

Use a host-partitioned, priority-aware URL frontier that leases eligible URLs to stateless fetchers; persist content durably, parse links asynchronously, deduplicate before re-admission, and continuously reschedule pages using change/importance signals while enforcing robots, politeness, budgets, and retries.
Partitioned append log or durable queue
Clarify scope, content types, continuous recrawl, robots/politeness
Estimate fetch rate, bandwidth, URL discovery amplification
URL frontier: priority + per-host queues + eligible-time heap

Memorize the architecture story: normalize/dedupe → host-aware frontier → leased fetch → durable store → parse/extract → re-admit links → adaptive recrawl. Then keep politeness, traps, retries, and ownership as your deep dives.

I would normalize and deduplicate every discovered URL before admitting it to a distributed URL frontier. The frontier is partitioned by host and combines priority with per-host next-eligible-time, so thousands of workers can crawl at high throughput without violating politeness. Workers receive leased tasks, check cached robots and DNS state, perform bounded HTTP fetches, persist raw content to object storage, and emit parse jobs. Parsers extract links that re-enter admission. Durable metadata tracks seen URLs, retries, content hashes, and fetch history; an adaptive recrawl scheduler revisits important or frequently changing pages. At scale I add backpressure, trap detection, host budgets, fencing for failover, and a separate browser-rendering pool for selected JavaScript pages.

Monitoring workloads are fundamentally time-series workloads: append-heavy ingestion, label-based filtering, range aggregation, retention/downsampling, and alert evaluation. The biggest traps are cardinality explosion, hot shards, expensive wide queries, and allowing the query/alert path to overload ingestion.
Push and/or pull numeric metrics with timestamp and labels
Graph metrics over time, group/filter by labels
Range, aggregation, rate, percentile, top-K, joins where supported

Design a highly available shopping cart service used across web and mobile. The cart must support anonymous and logged-in users, multi-device edits, quantity changes, save-for-later, item expiry, price refresh, promotion evaluation, cart merge at login, and a safe handoff into checkout without pretending the cart itself reserves inventory or locks price forever.

A shopping cart looks simple until concurrent devices, anonymous sessions, stale prices, limited inventory, promotion rules, and checkout races appear. The cart should remain highly available and user-friendly, while checkout performs authoritative validation of price, inventory and payment.

Adding an item to cart does NOT normally reserve inventory. The cart can show an availability hint, but authoritative availability/reservation occurs later, typically during checkout/order creation.
Phone reads cart quantity 1. Laptop reads quantity 1. Phone sets quantity 2. Laptop later writes stale full-cart document with quantity 1, erasing the phone update.
Use versioned conditional writes and intent-based operations. Laptop's stale replacement is rejected or rebased; ADD/REMOVE commands can merge according to defined semantics.

Store each cart as a versioned, partition-local document with stable line IDs and idempotent intent-based mutations; merge guest/user carts explicitly, treat price/inventory/promotion data as refreshable hints, and create an immutable checkout snapshot where authoritative price and stock validation begins.
CAS/retry merge against newest user cart
Requirements and cart vs checkout boundary

I would store each cart as a versioned document in a replicated KV store partitioned by cart ID. Use stable line IDs, intent-based mutations and idempotency keys so retries and multiple devices do not cause lost or duplicate updates. Guest and logged-in carts merge explicitly line-by-line at login. Catalog, price, inventory and promotion services enrich the cart, but price and stock are only hints until checkout; adding to cart normally does not reserve inventory. Checkout creates an immutable snapshot against an exact cart version and then performs authoritative price/inventory validation. Cart events publish asynchronously for analytics and reminders, while home-region writes simplify ordering and DR.

Design a global Amazon-style marketplace supporting product discovery, search, product detail pages, carts, inventory, checkout, payments, orders, shipment tracking, reviews, recommendations, sellers, promotions, and extreme events such as flash sales. The central challenge is combining read-heavy discovery with correctness-sensitive inventory, money, and order workflows.

Do not force one consistency model onto the whole system. Catalog/search/recommendations can be eventually consistent. Inventory reservation, payment state, order transitions, and idempotent checkout need much stronger correctness. The architecture should explicitly separate these worlds.

Address, shipping, tax, promotions, final quote

Product is the conceptual item, SKU is a purchasable variant, and Offer is a seller's commercial proposal for that SKU. A single phone model can have color/storage SKUs, and each SKU can have several seller offers with different price, condition, shipping promise, and fulfillment method.

A product page joins many domains. Building that page from normalized source tables on every request creates latency and coupling. Maintain denormalized read models for stable descriptive data, then overlay dynamic price/availability using bounded calls or cached summaries.

The same logical checkout retry must return the same order result and must not create a second order or second payment. Require a client-generated or server-issued idempotency key scoped to the shopper/checkout attempt.

For a strict-stock SKU/location, committed reservations must never exceed sellable stock. The exact implementation can use conditional atomic updates, row locks, compare-and-swap, or serialized partition processing.
If the checkout service times out after asking inventory to reserve, it must query by reservation_id before issuing another reservation. A timeout means the result is unknown.
Never infer payment failure merely from an HTTP timeout. The provider may have charged successfully. Use a merchant operation/idempotency key and query/reconcile provider state.

Active-active reads are easy compared with active-active inventory decrements and payment orchestration. Prefer explicit ownership/fencing for correctness-sensitive aggregates rather than casual multi-master writes.

Make discovery highly cached and eventually consistent, but funnel the purchase path through a durable idempotent workflow that atomically reserves scarce inventory, records immutable order/price facts, coordinates payment through recoverable state machines, and publishes side effects asynchronously.
Cart is intent; reserve briefly at checkout
One inventory row under flash sale

I would separate the read-heavy discovery path from the correctness-sensitive purchase path. Catalog and seller offers feed denormalized PDP models and a distributed search index; cart stores intent only. Checkout creates an authoritative quote and starts an idempotent saga. Inventory atomically creates short-lived reservations so scarce stock cannot be oversold. Order owns the lifecycle, payment uses provider idempotency plus UNKNOWN-state reconciliation, and order events are published through an outbox to fulfillment, notifications, analytics, and recommendations. Flash sales add CDN caching, waiting-room/admission control, queues, bot protection, and bounded stock tokens before the same checkout path. Global reads can be active-active, while inventory/order/payment use explicit ownership and fencing.

Distributed systems do not stay correct only because the happy-path code is correct. Timeouts, duplicate messages, operator mistakes, and external providers create ambiguous states. Reconciliation is a first-class correctness mechanism, especially for money and inventory.

textRun.content: The core difficulty is coordinating several independently changing actors—customer, restaurant, courier, payment provider, maps/ETA services—without using a giant distributed transaction. The design relies on explicit order state machines, idempotency, event-driven workflows, geospatial indexing, dispatch optimization, and reconciliation.
Discover restaurants, browse menus, cart, checkout, track, cancel, rate
Manage menu/availability, accept/reject order, update preparation status
Go online/offline, receive offers, accept/reject, pickup, navigate, deliver
Dispatch courier, calculate ETA/fees, payment, notifications, refunds, support
Monitor orders, intervene, reassign, issue credits/refunds, audit

Do not reconstruct an old order from the current menu. At checkout, snapshot item name, selected options, unit price, taxes/fees inputs, and menu/version metadata into the order. Restaurants may change price or remove an item seconds later; the accepted order must remain auditable.
Checkout request persisted; validate/payment path begins
Every transition checks current state/version. A stale duplicate command cannot move an order backward or repeat a terminal financial effect.
The final quoted checkout amount must have a quote/version/expiry. Payment and order persist the same accepted pricing breakdown so later recomputation does not change history.

Return existing order/payment for same idempotency key

Retry/backoff or fail checkout according to policy

If multiple couriers receive an offer, acceptance must use an atomic conditional assignment: delivery.courier_id changes from NULL to courier C only if still unassigned and offer valid. Losers receive 'offer no longer available'.

Customer cancellation and courier pickup arrive nearly simultaneously. The order workflow uses versioned state transitions. If PICKED_UP commits first, ordinary customer cancellation may be rejected/escalated. If CANCELLED commits first, pickup transition is rejected as stale and courier/restaurant compensation follows policy. Do not let two services independently overwrite the status.
Order service crashes after DB commit

Versioned/expiring; never silently recompute accepted order

Build the platform as a geo-partitioned event-driven marketplace: authoritative versioned order/payment/delivery state machines, a saga with transactional outbox, high-rate courier geo indexing, score-based dispatch with atomic assignment, and realtime tracking/ETA fan-out—while keeping search, notifications, analytics and settlement off the critical order path.
One checkout key -> one logical order

I would partition the marketplace by city/region and model order, payment and delivery as separate versioned state machines. Checkout revalidates the versioned menu and price, snapshots the order, creates it idempotently and authorizes payment. A durable saga coordinates restaurant acceptance, dispatch, pickup and delivery, while a transactional outbox reliably publishes every state change. Courier GPS streams into a geo-indexed latest-location store; dispatch queries nearby eligible couriers, scores them using prep time, ETA and acceptance probability, and uses a conditional update so only one courier wins. Tracking consumes location and order events to push ETA/status to customers. Retries, compensations, reconciliation and regional ownership make the workflow recoverable without distributed transactions.

tabs.title: Design Google Search / Web Search Engine

textRun.content: Design a large-scale web search engine that continuously discovers and crawls the public web, processes and deduplicates documents, builds distributed indexes, ranks results, and answers queries with very low latency. This is a pipeline-heavy system: crawling and indexing are asynchronous, while query serving is latency-critical.

Search is two giant systems joined together: an offline/nearline ingestion pipeline that converts the web into indexes, and an online distributed query engine that retrieves and ranks a tiny top-K from enormous immutable index data.

I’ll separate the system into crawl/index and query-serving planes. The crawl plane uses a durable URL frontier with per-host politeness, fetchers, parsing, duplicate detection, link extraction, and an incremental indexing pipeline. The serving plane shards an inverted index, retrieves candidates in parallel, merges top-K, applies ranking, and uses aggressive caching.
Find new URLs from seeds and extracted links
Parse, normalize, detect duplicates, extract links/text
Recrawl changing pages and update index
Minutes to days by page class
Do not obsess over exact Google numbers. Show that crawling, storage, indexing, and serving each operate at different scales, and that query serving cannot scan documents at request time.
Without canonicalization, the crawler wastes bandwidth fetching many syntactic URLs for the same logical page and pollutes the index with duplicates.
Important pages should be discovered/refreshed sooner
News/homepages change faster than archival pages
A crawler that maximizes throughput but overloads websites is badly designed. Host politeness is a first-class scheduling invariant.
Clean text, fields, language, canonical URL
Keep raw and processed data separate
Reprocessing parsers/ranking features should not require recrawling the internet. Durable raw snapshots let you rebuild downstream artifacts.
URL dedupe prevents refetching the same URL; content dedupe prevents indexing many URLs with the same or nearly identical content.
Readers can query a stable generation without locks while new segments are built separately. Publication is a metadata pointer change; compaction happens in background.
Each shard indexes subset of docs and all terms
Query fans to all shards; easy balanced corpus
Document-shard the corpus. Each shard computes its local top-K for the query, then an aggregator merges shard winners. Replicate shards for availability and query throughput.
Find thousands of plausible docs cheaply
You usually do not need to derive the equation. Explain term frequency, inverse document frequency, document-length normalization, and why lexical score is combined with other quality signals.
A common mistake is to say 'sort all matching documents'. Search engines aggressively avoid scoring and transferring candidates that cannot reach the first result page.
Median shard latency is not enough. Fan-out to hundreds/thousands of partitions amplifies tail latency, so p99 behavior and straggler mitigation become central.
Durable partition/replica restores queues and host state
Do not publish generation; retry missing segments
Serve older base with reduced freshness
All terms for subset of docs

Continuously turn the web into versioned immutable inverted indexes using a polite priority crawler and incremental processing pipeline, then answer each query by parallel retrieval across replicated document shards, aggressively prune to local top-K, globally merge/rerank, and use adaptive recrawling plus small fresh segments to keep results current.
Document is simpler for distributed top-K

Discover URL → canonicalize/seen check → priority/polite frontier → fetch → parse/dedupe/link extraction → incremental inverted index → replicated document shards → query parse → parallel retrieval → local top-K → global merge/rerank → snippets/results. Deep dives: frontier, inverted index, sharding, top-K, freshness, and tail latency.

I would split web search into a crawl/index plane and a query-serving plane. A durable URL frontier prioritizes discovery and recrawls while enforcing per-host robots and politeness. Fetchers store raw pages; parsers normalize text, extract links, and perform URL/content deduplication. Incremental indexers build immutable compressed inverted-index segments, with document-sharded replicas for serving. At query time, the frontend parses and normalizes the query, fans it to one replica of each document shard, each shard uses postings and early termination to return local top-K, and an aggregator merges and reranks a small global candidate set before generating snippets. Adaptive recrawling and fresh index segments provide freshness; caching, hedged requests, and replicas control latency and availability.

Design a Google Maps-style global mapping and navigation system. Users can browse maps, search places, request routes, receive turn-by-turn navigation, see live traffic, and share/update locations. The design must handle planetary-scale geospatial data, road graphs, enormous read traffic, frequent traffic updates, and low-latency routing.

I’ll split the design into map rendering, place/geospatial search, routing, and dynamic traffic/navigation. Static map and road data are heavily preprocessed and versioned. The online routing service searches a partitioned road graph using hierarchical speedups, while a separate streaming traffic pipeline continuously updates edge travel-time weights. Clients cache tiles and navigation state so temporary backend/network failures do not immediately stop guidance.
Route from A to B with alternatives
Road closures, map corrections, new places
Transit, Street View, satellite, offline maps
place_id, name, categories, lat/lng, address, geometry, metadata
edge_id, from, to, distance, speed limit, restrictions, geometry
incoming edge, outgoing edge, rule/time window
route, destination, progress, current matched edge
anonymous/session/device context, lat/lng, speed, heading, time
Map tiling, geospatial place search, and road routing are related but different problems. A tile grid is not a routing graph, and a geohash alone is not a shortest-path algorithm.
Use versioned vector tiles for roads, labels, boundaries, and POIs; raster/satellite imagery remains image tiles. Serve both through CDN.

Start with Dijkstra/A* for correctness, then explicitly explain the scale problem and introduce hierarchical preprocessing. That transition is usually more important than naming the fanciest algorithm.
Shortest distance, fastest route, and best ETA are different concepts. Routing optimizes a cost function; ETA estimates how long the chosen path will actually take.
For a maps design, privacy is architectural: traffic quality benefits from probes, but the system should not require retaining identifiable raw movement histories indefinitely.
CDN serves cached version; fail over origin
Replica serves; degrade optional ranking features
Route using older live state blended with historical
Dead reckoning / route progress estimation temporarily
Continue cached route; no fresh traffic/reroute
Routing continues without freshest incident layer
Client retains current route and maneuvers

Precompute and version the mostly static world—tiles, place indexes, road topology, and routing hierarchy—then continuously overlay dynamic traffic weights from privacy-controlled map-matched probes, allowing regional routing services to compute fast hierarchical shortest paths and clients to navigate reliably with cached route state.
Vector for dynamic styling; raster for imagery

Map data → versioned vector tiles/search index/road graph → CDN and regional services. Route request → snap to roads → hierarchical search with traffic-weighted edges → ETA/instructions. GPS probes → map matching → edge speed aggregation → live/predictive traffic weights → reroute only when useful.

I would separate mostly static map data from highly dynamic traffic. The map pipeline publishes immutable vector/raster tiles, place/geocoder indexes, and a partitioned directed road graph with hierarchical routing shortcuts. Tiles are CDN-served. For directions, the service snaps endpoints to roads and uses hierarchical A*/shortest-path search rather than plain Dijkstra over the entire graph. GPS and sensor probes flow through map matching and windowed aggregation to produce live edge speeds, which are blended with historical/predicted traffic for routing and ETA. Navigation clients cache the route and maneuvers, progress locally, and request rerouting only on real deviation, closure, or meaningful time savings. Dynamic closure overlays, regional replicas, and offline/client fallback keep core navigation available.

textRun.content: Design a low-latency electronic exchange that accepts buy/sell orders, enforces deterministic price-time priority, matches orders without double execution, publishes market data, survives failures without corrupting the order book, and provides a complete auditable event trail.
Why this is a new problem

Cloud file sync and ticket booking were already covered earlier, so this problem intentionally moves to a different architecture: deterministic single-writer matching, in-memory order books, write-ahead event logs, replay, market-data sequencing, and exchange-grade risk controls.
Cancel open order or modify according to exchange rules
Maintain bids and asks per instrument
Best bid/ask, depth, trades, sequence numbers
client_order_id, account, instrument, side, type, price, qty, tif
An order's executed quantity + remaining quantity + cancelled/expired remainder must reconcile to the accepted quantity, subject to explicit replace semantics.
Highest price first; FIFO within same price
Lowest price first; FIFO within same price
Better price wins first. At the same price, the earlier accepted order wins. This must be deterministic and based on exchange order, not client timestamps.
Find best price and insert/remove levels
Accepted order can vanish on crash
Machine loss may still lose unreplicated tail
Put deterministic, necessary risk checks on the critical path; send heavier analytics and surveillance asynchronously. Cache reference/limit data close to the gateway/engine.
Remain across sessions per venue rules
Execute entire quantity immediately or none
Must add liquidity; reject/cancel if it would cross

Order O is resting. A marketable order and O's cancel arrive nearly simultaneously. Do not use locks/timestamps to guess. The sequencer establishes a total order for that book. If match command is first, the eligible quantity fills; if cancel is first, it is removed before matching.
Best default; each book has one owner
Bad for matching because both sides meet on same book

Do not run two independent active matching engines for the same instrument in different regions. They could both fill the same resting order. One active owner per book is the simplest correctness model.
Retry deduplicated by client/session order ID
Replay produces same fill/trade ID or authoritative output log prevents duplicate effect
Do not promote beyond known committed point without defined recovery
Matching continues; publisher rebuilds from event log/snapshot
Buffer immutable trade events; matching policy independent

Given snapshot at sequence 1,000,000 and commands 1,000,001..1,100,000, a recovered engine must produce the same final book and execution results as the original engine. Nondeterministic iteration order, wall-clock-dependent matching, random IDs, or concurrency inside one book can break this.

Shard by instrument, give each order book one fenced single-writer matching owner, sequence and durably journal commands, match entirely in memory with deterministic price-time priority, then publish executions and market-data deltas asynchronously while snapshots plus replay provide recovery.

Keep the matching loop conceptually simple. The sophistication is in deterministic ordering, durability, recovery, hot-path isolation and failover, not in turning the algorithm into a distributed transaction.
No resting crossed book after event

I would shard the exchange by instrument and give each order book exactly one fenced active matching owner. Order gateways authenticate members and run pre-trade checks, then commands are sequenced and durably journaled according to the venue's acceptance contract. The matching engine keeps bids and asks in memory and processes one ordered event stream using deterministic price-time priority, including partial fills, cancels and replaces. It emits immutable trades, execution reports and book deltas. Market data is published independently with sequence numbers and snapshot/gap recovery. Periodic snapshots plus journal replay recover an engine, while fencing prevents split-brain ownership. Clearing, surveillance and analytics consume the authoritative event stream asynchronously.
Ordered tree/skip structure or bounded price ladder
O(1) to O(log P) depending representation
O(log P), or O(1) in indexed ladder

Immediate if cancel event wins sequence

tabs.title: Design Google Docs / Real-Time Collaborative Edit…

textRun.content: Design a collaborative document editor where many users can edit the same document concurrently, see changes with low latency, reconnect safely, work offline, preserve a durable revision history, and converge to the same document despite reordering, retries and failures.

The difficult part is not storing text. It is defining how concurrent edits are ordered or merged so every replica converges without losing user intent. Separate the realtime collaboration stream from durable snapshots, revision history, permissions, search and exports.

If Alice and Bob both edit revision 10 and every client simply applies remote positions literally, character offsets shift and replicas can diverge. The system needs Operational Transformation, CRDTs, or another formally defined convergence mechanism.

Base text ABC. Alice inserts X at position 1; Bob concurrently inserts Y at position 2. If Alice's insert commits first, Bob's insert position may transform from 2 to 3 so it still targets the original logical location.
Inserted content inherits/doesn't inherit style by rule
Formatting range shrinks around deleted content

Choose one primary model and go deep. For a Google-Docs-like centralized service, OT with one logical document leader is easy to explain. Mention CRDT as an alternative and compare its offline/convergence trade-offs.
Compaction must never make an active client's base revision impossible to reconcile. Keep enough transform/history state or force that client through a full resync.

Alice is editing while the owner revokes her access. The ACL update becomes authoritative, invalidates active collaboration sessions, and the document leader rejects subsequent operations from Alice. Already committed operations remain in history; uncommitted local edits should be preserved client-side for copy/recovery rather than silently discarded.
Client reconnects and syncs from revision
Leader dies after commit before ACK
Operation log remains source of truth

Use local-first clients, a fenced per-document collaboration leader, deterministic OT (or a clearly chosen CRDT alternative), an idempotent durable operation log plus snapshots, revision-based reconnect, and separate ephemeral presence/fan-out so concurrent and offline edits converge without putting storage or slow clients on the keystroke path.
Locally applied operation sent but not ACKed
New local edits created while pending exists
Transform remote against pending/buffer and vice versa
You do not need to derive a complete OT algebra on the whiteboard. You do need to demonstrate that stale numeric positions cannot be applied directly and show one correct transformed example.

I would make editing local-first and route each active document to one fenced collaboration leader. Clients send stable operation IDs with a base revision over persistent connections. Using OT, the leader transforms stale operations against canonical edits committed since that base, assigns a new revision, durably appends the operation, and only then ACKs and broadcasts it. Clients reconcile remote operations with their pending local edits so every replica converges. Periodic snapshots compact the operation log; reconnect uses missing operations or snapshot plus rebase, including offline edits. Presence/cursors use separate ephemeral pub-sub, assets use object storage, ACL changes invalidate sessions, and replicated logs plus fencing handle leader/region failure.
